title: Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B: Alibaba's Largest Model Launches
summary: Alibaba Cloud's Qwen Team officially released Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B on August 12, 2026. Explore the 2.4 trillion parameter architecture and enterprise capabilities.
body_text: Alibaba Cloud's Qwen Team has officially launched Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B, a massive 2.4 trillion parameter large language model released on August 12, 2026. The model leverages mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture with 95 billion active parameters, positioning Alibaba to compete directly with frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google in the enterprise AI segment. Architecture and Scale Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B represents a significant architectural leap in Alibaba's language model portfolio. The model deploys 2.4 trillion total parameters while activating only 95 billion parameters per forward pass through its MoE routing system. This design choice allows the model to maintain inference efficiency while accessing the knowledge capacity of a substantially larger parameter base. The "A95B" designation in the model name explicitly references the 95 billion active parameter count, a transparency move that distinguishes total parameters from compute-active parameters during inference. This architecture follows the industry trend toward sparse models that balance capability with operational cost, similar to approaches used in Google's Switch Transformer and Mistral's Mixtral series. Release Date and Availability Officially launched on August 12, 2026, Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B is now available through Alibaba Cloud's model service platform. The release operates under the Qwen3_8_Max license, which governs commercial usage terms and redistribution policies for enterprise customers. Alibaba has positioned this launch as part of its broader Qwen3.8 model family, which spans multiple parameter scales and specialization domains. Enterprise Positioning The model targets enterprise customers requiring advanced reasoning, multilingual support, and domain-specific task performance. Key capabilities reportedly include: Multi-turn conversation handling with extended context windows Cross-lingual understanding across Chinese, English, and additional Asian languages Code generation and technical documentation analysis Business intelligence and data interpretation tasks Alibaba Cloud has optimized the model for deployment within its cloud infrastructure, offering managed inference endpoints and fine-tuning services. This integrated approach aims to reduce implementation friction for enterprises already operating within Alibaba's ecosystem, particularly across Asia-Pacific markets where Alibaba maintains strong cloud infrastructure presence. Competitive Landscape The Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B launch intensifies competition in the trillion-parameter model category. While Western labs like OpenAI and Anthropic dominate headlines in North American and European markets, Alibaba's Qwen series has established significant traction in Chinese and Southeast Asian enterprise deployments. The 2.4 trillion parameter scale places this model among the largest commercially available language models, though direct performance comparisons remain limited pending independent benchmark evaluations. The mixture-of-experts architecture suggests Alibaba is prioritizing inference cost management, a critical factor for enterprise customers processing high query volumes. By activating only 95 billion parameters per inference pass, the model potentially offers better cost-per-token economics than dense models of equivalent capability, though actual performance metrics will determine real-world competitiveness. What This Means Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B signals Alibaba Cloud's commitment to competing at the frontier of large language model development. For enterprises operating in Asia-Pacific regions or requiring strong Chinese language capabilities, this model provides a domestically-developed alternative to US-based foundation models. The MoE architecture and explicit active parameter labeling reflect industry maturation toward transparent, cost-efficient model design. Organizations evaluating the model should conduct domain-specific benchmarks to assess performance against their particular use cases before committing to production deployments.

title: Shark® Launches AquaReach™, the First Vacuum & Mop System with Extendable Wand Designed to Clean Beyond the Floor
summary: Shark® Launches AquaReach™, the First Vacuum & Mop System with Extendable Wand Designed to Clean Beyond the Floor. The latest on SharkNinja innovations—press releases, product launches, media kits, images, and press contacts.
body_text: An integrated extendable wand brings wet & dry cleaning from hard floors to baseboards, windowsills, cabinet fronts, and more. NEEDHAM, Mass.–(BUSINESS WIRE)– SharkNinja, Inc. (NYSE: SN), a global product design and technology company, today announced Shark® AquaReach™, the industry’s first wet & dry cleaner designed to clean more than just your floors. AquaReach™ vacuums and mops hard floors at the same time, then extends its reach with an integrated wand to clean hard-to-reach areas like baseboards, windowsills, cabinet fronts and other hard surfaces. AquaReach™ Pro includes a Total Self-Cleaning and Drying System. Across TikTok and social media, consumers have shared countless cleaning hacks to reach the places other floor cleaners may not reach—wrapping towels around mops, taping microfiber cloths to cleaning tools and inventing DIY workarounds just to finish the job. Those videos weren’t just clever hacks; they revealed an unmet need. “People weren’t creating cleaning hacks because they wanted to—they were creating them because they had to,” said Petra Oman, VP of Marketing at SharkNinja. “They showed us what was missing. AquaReach™ was built around the way people were already cleaning, combining vacuuming, mopping and extended reach so they can tackle more of the mess in one routine.” Built for Real Life. And Real Messes. Real-life messes don’t stay on the floor. Smoothie splatter ends up on cabinet fronts. Crayon streaks find their way onto tile grout. Grime builds up in the tight spaces around the toilet. On the floor, AquaReach™ tackles wet and dry messes at the same time. The brushroll rotates continuously, working with a powerful jet of cleaning solution to loosen and scrub stuck-on debris, while Shark’s powerful suction lifts away dirt and dirty liquid simultaneously. When it’s time to clean beyond the floor, the integrated extendable wand brings the same vacuuming and mopping power to surfaces the nozzle can’t reach with two specialized tools: Stain Scrubber: Targeted spray and powerful suction remove stuck-on messes 2x faster* from the floor, baseboards, windowsills, behind toilets and bathtub ledges. Detailer Mop: Reaches under furniture, along edges and into tight corners for targeted mopping and debris pickup. Always Ready for the Next Clean AquaReach™ continuously refreshes its brushroll while cleaning to help prevent dirty water and debris from being redeposited onto floors. A dual-tank system keeps clean and dirty water separate, while an on-dock rinse cycle flushes the brushroll after every use, so it’s ready for the next clean. AquaReach™ Pro adds the Total Self-Cleaning and Drying System. Its Self-Sanitizing** dock rinses the brushroll and dries it with heated air up to 160°F, helping reduce odors and eliminating 99.9% of bacteria from the brushroll.*** Additional features include: Edge-Optimized Nozzle: Cleans closer to baseboards and edges, reducing missed spots and minimizing touch-ups. LED Reveal Beam: Illuminates hidden dust, crumbs, hair and debris so nothing gets left behind. Availability Shark® AquaReach™ ($399.99) and AquaReach™ Pro ($529.99) are both available starting today on SharkNinja.com and TikTok Shop, with additional color and retail availability coming in the upcoming weeks. About SharkNinja SharkNinja is a global product design and technology company, with a diversified portfolio of 5-star rated lifestyle solutions that positively impact people’s lives in homes around the world. Powered by two trusted, global brands, Shark and Ninja, the company has a proven track record of bringing disruptive innovation to market, and developing one consumer product after another has allowed SharkNinja to enter multiple product categories, driving significant growth and market share gains. Headquartered in Needham, Massachusetts with more than 4,100 associates, the company’s products are sold at key retailers, online and offline, and through distributors around the world. For more information, please visit sharkninja.com . * Based on IEC 62885-6 5.1 Aqua Reach wand vs. nozzle. ** Bacterial reduction on brush-roll, tested in External Lab under controlled conditions. In-home results may vary. When used as directed. *** Bacterial reduction on brush-roll, tested in External Lab under controlled conditions. In-home results may vary. title: No Minimum Order: Start China Sourcing With One Unit
summary: You can source from China one unit at a time. What MOQ really means, four no-minimum routes for Pakistani sellers, and when to buy in bulk instead.
body_text: Yes, you can buy from China one unit at a time. Minimum order quantity — MOQ — is a supplier's rule, not a law of importing, and several routes into the Chinese market ignore it completely: paid samples, agent-bought 1688 and Taobao items, and dropshipping catalogues that ship a single piece to your customer's door. The catch is price per unit. A factory quotes its lowest rate at volume, so one piece always costs more per piece than a carton would. What that premium buys you is information — whether the product actually sells, whether the quality survives the trip, and whether Pakistani buyers accept it at the door — before you put real money into stock. This guide covers what MOQ really is, four ways around it from Pakistan, what a single unit costs once it lands, how to negotiate a smaller first order, and when bulk is the better call. What MOQ means, and why suppliers set one MOQ is the smallest quantity a supplier will sell in one order. It is quoted per product, and often per variant — a supplier may accept a small total order but insist on a set quantity per colour or size. The reasons are usually real, not greed: Setup cost. Changing a machine over to your product takes time whether you order fifty pieces or five thousand. That cost is spread across the run. Materials. Fabric comes on rolls, plastic in bags, boxes in print runs. Small orders leave awkward leftovers. Packaging. Printed cartons and labels have their own minimums, often higher than the product's. Admin. Quoting, invoicing, packing and export paperwork cost the same on a tiny order as on a large one. Which is why MOQ varies so much by who you are actually talking to. A factory that manufactures the item wants a production run. A trading company that buys from that factory and holds stock can break a carton. A wholesale market seller in Yiwu or Guangzhou will sell you a handful. And a marketplace that has already imported the goods will sell you one. So the useful question is never "what is the MOQ for this product?" It is "who is the cheapest person in this chain who will sell me the quantity I need?" Four ways to buy a single unit from China 1. Order a sample Nearly every serious supplier on Alibaba sells samples, and this is the most direct answer to the no-minimum question. You pay a higher per-piece price, often plus courier, and you get the exact item you were about to commit to. Many suppliers will credit the sample cost against a later bulk order — ask before you pay, and get the answer in writing on the platform. Samples are worth the premium because they answer questions a listing photo cannot: real material, real weight, real finish, real packaging. If you are new to the platform, our step-by-step on ordering from Alibaba to Pakistan covers payment and shipping mechanics, and Alibaba in Pakistan covers what the platform does and does not do for buyers here. 2. Buy through a China-based agent 1688 and Taobao are China's domestic platforms. Prices sit close to wholesale and minimums are often tiny or non-existent, because these sites were built for Chinese buyers rather than exporters. The obstacles are practical: Chinese-language listings, Chinese payment methods, and sellers who only ship to a domestic address. Sourcing agents and freight forwarders exist to bridge exactly that. The agent buys on your behalf, receives the item at their warehouse, checks it, and forwards it to Pakistan — usually consolidating several purchases into one shipment. You pay a service fee plus domestic and international shipping on top of the product price. This route gives you the widest product range at the lowest sticker price, and the highest number of moving parts. Our roundup of the best China wholesale websites for Pakistan compares which platform suits which kind of buyer. 3. Buy from a catalogue that already imported it The simplest route: let someone else carry the MOQ. When a platform has already imported a product, cleared it and holds it, the minimum order stops being a factory question. You order one piece at the listed price and it ships. That is how China sourcing works on Markaz China — no minimum order anywhere in the catalogue, a landed price in PKR rather than a foreign sticker price plus unknowns, cash on delivery collected from your customer, and a China-to-door delivery window of roughly 10 to 17 days. You skip the freight quote, the customs paperwork and the currency conversion, and you pay for that in a per-unit price that sits above a factory's bulk rate. The honest comparison is in our breakdown of sourcing from China for Pakistani resellers : Alibaba and Yiwu win on sticker price at volume, catalogue sourcing wins when the order is one unit and the freight, duty and risk would otherwise be yours alone. 4. Split an order with other resellers If a supplier will not go below a set quantity and you only want a share, group buying is the old workaround: three or four sellers combine to hit the MOQ and split the carton on arrival. It works, and it goes wrong in predictable ways. Agree in advance who pays the freight, who holds the goods, who deals with the supplier if a batch is faulty, and what happens if one person's share does not sell. Do it with people you actually know, not names from a group chat. What one unit really costs to land in Pakistan The product price is the smallest part of a single-unit import. The number that matters is landed cost per unit, and it stacks up like this: The item price, at sample or single-piece rate rather than bulk rate. Domestic shipping inside China, from the seller to your agent's warehouse. The agent's service fee, if you used one. International freight — priced by actual or volumetric weight, whichever is greater, and usually with a minimum billable weight. Duties and taxes on arrival, which depend on the product category and the declared value. Last-mile delivery inside Pakistan, plus any COD handling on the way back out. Payment and currency conversion costs. Freight is what punishes single units hardest. A courier's minimum billable weight and fixed handling charges do not shrink because your parcel is small, so the per-unit share of shipping on a one-piece order can rival the item itself — especially for anything bulky and light, where volumetric weight decides the bill. Worked example — use your own live quotes, never numbers copied from an article: take the supplier's single-piece price. Add the domestic China leg and the agent fee. Add the international freight for that parcel, using the greater of actual and volumetric weight. Add duty and taxes as quoted for that category. Divide the total by one, because you bought one. Now compare that figure with the same product's wholesale price in a Pakistani market, and with the landed PKR price of the nearest item in a China product category . Sometimes the import wins. On heavy, cheap, commodity items, it very often does not — and it is far better to learn that on paper than after paying freight. The full mechanics of the import route, including paperwork and clearance, are in our guide to importing products from China to Pakistan . How to get a supplier to lower its minimum Published MOQs are an opening position more often than sellers assume. A few things move them: Ask with a number. "What is your MOQ?" invites the standard answer. "Can you do a first order of X pieces, with a larger repeat order if it sells?" invites a real one. Take stock colours and sizes. Custom variants force a production run. Whatever is already on the shelf can be broken into small quantities. Drop the branding on the first order. Printed boxes and logo work carry their own minimums, and they are usually what is holding the MOQ up. Brand later, once the product has proven itself. Our guide to packaging and branding for small online sellers covers what can be done locally instead. Pay the sample price without haggling. Arguing over a sample marks you as a buyer who will argue over everything. Paying it cleanly buys goodwill on the real order. Go one step down the chain. If the factory will not break its run, its stockist or a trading company probably will, at a slightly higher per-piece price. Say what you are doing. Suppliers deal with test buyers constantly. "I am testing this product in Pakistan and will reorder if it sells" is a normal, credible message. Keep it all on the platform. Chat, quotes, agreed specification, payment. The moment a conversation moves to a private wallet or a personal account, your protection goes with it — the warning signs are listed in is it safe to order from China in Pakistan . The single-unit test loop A one-piece order is not a purchase, it is an experiment. Run it like one. Pick one product with a clear buyer. Not five. One test at a time is the only way to know what the answer applies to. Order the single unit by whichever of the four routes above fits the product. Inspect it properly when it lands. Build quality, does it match the listing, how it survived the box, size and weight against your courier's slabs, and anything that needs a plug, a voltage or an instruction sheet a Pakistani buyer can read. Shoot your own photos and one video with that unit. Supplier images sell a product nobody believes; your own hand holding it sells one they do. List it and run it for two weeks on the channels you already use, at a price built from your real landed cost. Count the outcomes. Enquiries, orders, and how many of those orders were actually accepted at the door. A product with orders and heavy refusals is not a winner. Then decide. Reorder in quantity, retest at a different price, or drop it and keep the unit as a demo piece. Choosing what to test first matters more than the testing. Our list of the best products to source from China is a sensible shortlist to start from, and small, light, non-fragile items are the cheapest things to be wrong about. When buying in bulk is the right answer Single-unit sourcing is a testing tool, not a business model. Switch to volume when: The product has proven demand. Once orders are steady, the per-unit freight premium is pure lost margin. Freight dominates the item price. Heavy or bulky goods only make sense consolidated into one shipment. You want your own branding. Custom packaging and logos need a production run, full stop. Timing is fixed. Seasonal stock has to be here before the season, not somewhere over the Arabian Sea during it. Your buyers will not wait. Shipping from China runs around 10 to 17 days door to door; local Markaz stock runs 3 to 5 days. If your customers expect a parcel this week, you need stock in Pakistan — the trade-offs are laid out in how long China-to-Pakistan delivery takes . The sequence that wastes the least money is simple: test single units, sell from a no-minimum catalogue while demand is unproven, and place a bulk order only for the products that have already earned it. Running no-MOQ sourcing through Markaz If you would rather not manage agents, freight and clearance while you are still finding out what sells, this is the shortcut. Every product in the China deals catalogue can be ordered as a single unit. The price you see is the landed PKR price, the supplier ships, your customer pays cash on delivery, and the money is settled to you. Local products work the same way. Browse the Markaz shop for stock already inside Pakistan on a 3 to 5 day delivery window, and use the dropshipping portal to place orders and track dispatches in one place instead of across chat threads. It is not the cheapest per unit — nothing that carries the MOQ for you is — and it is the least expensive way to be wrong about a product. If you are still weighing supplier options, our comparison of the best dropshipping suppliers in Pakistan puts the local and China-sourced routes side by side. Mistakes that make single-unit sourcing expensive Testing ten products at once from ten suppliers. You pay the fixed freight and handling cost ten times. Consolidate through one agent, or test in sequence. Testing heavy, cheap items. The shipping on a single bulky unit can exceed the product's retail price here. Start light. Pricing retail off the sample cost. The sample rate is not your future cost base, and it is not your bulk rate either. Price the test to learn, and reprice on real numbers when you reorder. Skipping the drop test. Anything glass, ceramic or hinged has to survive a Pakistani last-mile delivery, not just the flight. Find that out on one unit. Paying outside the platform. A discount for paying into a personal account is not a discount. Never photographing the unit. If the test ends and you have no photos, video or measurements of your own, you paid for the item and threw away the reason you bought it. Start with one unit No minimum order sourcing is not a loophole. It is the sensible order of operations: buy one, look at it, sell it, count what happened, and only then commit money to a carton. Pick one product this week. Get a single unit of it into your hands by whichever route is cheapest for that item. The information is worth more than the premium you paid for it.

body_text: The search for the origins of life has taken scientists far beyond Earth, and a surprising discovery in deep space may provide important answers. Researchers have detected a natural sugar molecule floating between stars in the Milky Way, a finding that could change how scientists understand the formation of the ingredients needed for life. The molecule, called erythrulose, has been identified inside an interstellar molecular cloud near the centre of our galaxy. On Earth, the same sugar can be found naturally in some foods, including raspberries, and it is also associated with products such as artificial tanning formulas. While discovering sugar in space may sound unusual, scientists say the finding has major implications. Sugars are essential components of living systems. They are involved in the structure of genetic materials such as DNA and RNA and play important roles in biological processes that allow life to function. The discovery raises a fascinating possibility: some of the chemical ingredients required for life may have existed in space before Earth itself was formed. A New Discovery in the Chemistry of Space For decades, astronomers have studied the complex molecules that exist in the space between stars, known as the interstellar medium. These regions contain clouds of gas and dust where stars and planets are eventually formed. Scientists have already discovered a variety of organic molecules in space, including some compounds linked to the chemistry of life. Sugars have also been detected in meteorite samples collected on Earth, suggesting that some life-related molecules may have arrived from space. However, finding a sugar molecule directly in interstellar space is a much more significant discovery. It provides evidence that complex organic compounds can form naturally in the cold environments between stars. Researchers identified erythrulose in a molecular cloud known as G+0.693−0.027, located close to the centre of the Milky Way galaxy. The discovery was made through highly sensitive observations using advanced radio telescopes capable of detecting the chemical fingerprints of molecules across enormous distances. By comparing the signals detected from space with laboratory measurements of erythrulose, scientists were able to confirm that the molecular pattern matched. Why Sugars Matter in the Search for Life Sugars are among the most important molecules in biology. They are not simply sources of energy but also provide the framework for some of the most fundamental processes of life. DNA and RNA, the molecules responsible for storing and transferring genetic information, rely on sugar-based structures. Because of this, scientists have long wondered how these essential compounds first appeared on the early Earth. One major question in astrochemistry is whether the building blocks of life formed on Earth or whether some arrived from space. The discovery of erythrulose supports the idea that space environments may naturally create complex organic molecules. These compounds could have later become part of planets, moons, asteroids, and other celestial bodies. When Earth was young, it experienced a period known as the Late Heavy Bombardment, when large numbers of asteroids and other space objects struck the planet. Researchers suggest that organic molecules carried by these objects may have contributed to the chemical ingredients available on early Earth. According to estimates from the research team, enormous quantities of this sugar could potentially have reached Earth during that ancient period. Challenging Previous Ideas About Space Chemistry The discovery also challenges some existing theories about how molecules develop in space. Scientists previously believed that interstellar molecules generally became more complex through a gradual process where carbon atoms were added one after another. However, erythrulose does not completely fit that pattern. Researchers found that this four-carbon sugar appeared to be more common than some simpler three-carbon sugars that were expected to appear first. “This finding was unexpected,” researchers noted, suggesting that chemical reactions in space may be more complicated than previously understood. The result could encourage scientists to rethink how organic molecules form in environments far from planets. Could This Help Find Alien Life? The discovery does not prove that life exists elsewhere in the universe. Finding a sugar molecule in space is not the same as finding living organisms or evidence of alien biology. However, it does show that some of the chemical ingredients associated with life are not unique to Earth. If complex organic molecules can form naturally in space, it increases the possibility that similar chemistry may occur on other planets and moons. Scientists studying places such as Mars, Europa, and Enceladus are particularly interested in understanding whether the conditions needed for life could exist elsewhere. Future discoveries of organic molecules in different space environments may help answer one of humanity’s biggest questions: how common is life in the universe? The Future of Astrochemistry Research Modern telescopes are allowing scientists to explore the universe in greater detail than ever before. Instead of only observing stars and planets, researchers can now study the chemical composition of distant regions of space. The discovery of erythrulose demonstrates how much remains unknown about the origins of organic chemistry. Every new molecule found between stars provides another piece of the puzzle. Scientists will continue searching for more complex compounds that may reveal how the chemistry of life began. These discoveries could eventually explain whether Earth’s life was a rare accident or a natural outcome of the universe’s chemistry. The discovery of sugar in deep space is therefore more than a scientific curiosity. It represents a possible connection between the chemistry of the cosmos and the emergence of life on our planet. Disclaimer This article is based on publicly available scientific reporting and research information. The discovery of organic molecules in space does not confirm the existence of extraterrestrial life. Scientific interpretations may change as new evidence becomes available. Sources Jimenez Serra et al., “Detection of a chiral four-carbon sugar in interstellar space,” Nature Astronomy (2026). Reporting based on coverage from The Independent, IndyTech , August 2026. Research and astronomical observations conducted using data from advanced radio telescope surveys studying interstellar molecular clouds.

title: The Most Compute-Hungry Frontier
summary: From AlphaFold to weather, materials, and fusion, AI for science couples models with simulation and screening, making it among the most compute-hungry work in computing.
body_text: AI for science has become the most compute-hungry frontier in computing, and it is only accelerating. The systems now reshaping biology, weather, materials, fusion, and mathematics share one structure. Each pairs a trained model with a physics simulation or solver, then runs it at enormous scale. That combination makes scientific AI at least as demanding as serving a large language model, and far more sustained. Drug discovery is the most visible example. Even so, it is only the start. Key finding: Scientific AI is voracious because it pairs models with simulation and runs them at planetary scale. AlphaFold predicted more than 200 million protein structures and won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. GNoME predicted 2.2 million new crystals. GraphCast produces a 10-day global forecast in under a minute. Unlike a chatbot, each scientific inference is itself a computation, repeated millions of times. 200M+ Protein structures predicted by AlphaFold 2.2M New crystals predicted by GNoME (380k likely stable) < 1 min A 10-day global weather forecast on one machine AI Has Become an Instrument of Discovery Something fundamental has shifted in how science gets done. AI is no longer only a tool for summarising papers or writing code. Instead, it has become an instrument of discovery in its own right, on par with the microscope or the particle accelerator. A 2023 review in Nature made the point plainly. Led by Hanchen Wang, with co-authors including Yoshua Bengio and Marinka Zitnik, it showed that machine learning is now woven through the scientific method itself, from generating hypotheses to interpreting results. The recognition is official. In 2024, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for AlphaFold, and to David Baker for computational protein design. A method that did not exist a decade ago now sits in the canon of chemistry. Behind every one of these breakthroughs, however, is a fact that rarely makes the headline. Each one runs on an enormous amount of compute. Drug Discovery: From Decades to Days Start with the field that made the case. For fifty years, determining a single protein’s three-dimensional shape could take a graduate student most of a PhD. AlphaFold collapsed that timeline. By 2024 it had predicted the structures of more than 200 million proteins, very nearly every protein known to science. The public database had already been used by over two million researchers in 190 countries. Structure is only the opening move. Modern drug discovery now chains several AI workloads together. Generative models propose candidate molecules, structure models predict how they bind, and molecular dynamics simulates the interaction over time. Each stage is GPU-bound, and the screening step runs across millions of compounds. Axe Compute’s own subsidiary, Predictive Oncology, applies AI to this problem in cancer research. For us, in other words, the economics of scientific compute are close to home. The point for infrastructure is the shape of the workload. This is not a single model answering a single question. Instead, it is a pipeline of training, simulation, and large-scale inference. As a result, it runs for weeks and saturates whatever hardware it is given. Weather and Climate: Physics at the Speed of Inference Weather prediction has been the domain of physics-based supercomputers for half a century. That is changing. In 2023, DeepMind’s GraphCast, published in Science , produced 10-day global forecasts in under a minute on a single machine. Moreover, it outperformed the European Centre’s gold-standard High-Resolution Forecast on 90 percent of 1,380 verification targets. The speed is dramatic, yet it hides the compute. Training a model like GraphCast means learning from decades of reanalysis data. The most capable successors then run large probabilistic ensembles, generating many possible futures rather than one. So the fast inference rests on a heavy, sustained training and ensemble pipeline. That split between training and inference is even sharper here than in enterprise AI, a distinction we examine in Training vs Inference Infrastructure . Materials: Eight Hundred Years of Discovery in One Run In November 2023, DeepMind published GNoME in Nature . This graph neural network predicted 2.2 million new crystal structures, which the team described as roughly 800 years’ worth of discovery. About 380,000 are predicted to be stable enough to be worth synthesising. External laboratories have already made hundreds of them, and a Berkeley Lab robotic facility synthesised dozens autonomously. What makes this compute-hungry is the loop. GNoME generates candidate crystals, then validates them with density-functional theory, an established but expensive physics calculation. The results feed back through active learning. DeepMind reported that this raised the discovery rate from under 10 percent to over 80 percent. That efficiency, the team noted, directly affects how much compute each discovery costs. In effect, materials science has become a search problem run at a scale only GPUs make feasible. Fusion and Mathematics: Control and Proof Two further fields show how wide the frontier has become. In 2022, DeepMind and the Swiss Plasma Center at EPFL published work in Nature on fusion control. A deep reinforcement-learning controller held plasma inside a live tokamak, reading 90 measurements and adjusting 19 magnets ten thousand times a second. Notably, the controller was trained entirely in simulation before it ever touched the reactor. That is a compute cost paid upfront, so the physical experiment can run safely. Mathematics has joined too. In 2024, DeepMind’s AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry 2 reached a silver-medal score at the International Mathematical Olympiad. They solved four of six problems, for 28 points out of 42. AlphaProof pairs a language model with the reinforcement-learning approach behind AlphaZero. Crucially, it leans on inference-time search, spending large amounts of compute to reason toward a proof. That is the same test-time compute dynamic now reshaping the economics of AI more broadly. The Common Thread: Why Science Eats Compute Across all of these fields, the pattern is identical. A scientific AI system is a trained model wrapped around a simulation or solver. It runs at a scale that turns discovery into a search. That is a different machine from a chatbot, and it consumes compute differently. A language model serves one short burst of inference to a human reader, then sits idle. A scientific model’s inference is the experiment itself: folding a protein, simulating a plasma step, or screening a compound. That work repeats millions or billions of times, often coupled to a physics calculation that is itself GPU-bound. It is sustained, not spiky, and it does not pause between queries. The hardware trend makes this harder, not easier. Epoch AI has shown that training compute for the largest models doubles roughly every six months, far faster than hardware efficiency improves. At the same time, memory bandwidth has fallen behind raw arithmetic. Researchers call this gap the memory wall, and it bites hardest on the large, data-heavy models that science now relies on. More science means more compute, and the compute is getting harder to feed. What Scientific AI Teams Need from Infrastructure Axe Compute operates across 200+ locations worldwide on 400,000+ existing GPUs. Axe Compute does not add any egress fees with pricing that is significantly below hyperscaler rates. Scientific workloads have specific demands. Molecular dynamics and large foundation models need high-memory GPUs. Tightly coupled simulation and distributed training need high-bandwidth interconnect such as InfiniBand. Research data is often regulated or sovereign. As a result, capacity has to sit in a named jurisdiction rather than wherever a hyperscaler has space. Above all, this work needs sustained, predictable capacity, not spot instances that disappear mid-run. Historically, that combination has been hard for anyone outside a national lab or a hyperscaler to assemble. That is part of why so much frontier science concentrates in a few institutions. The way out is choice. With Axe Compute, a research team selects the region, GPU type, and network fabric it needs through the Build program. It can then reserve dedicated bare-metal capacity in about 48 hours, rather than waiting quarters for hardware. For teams planning how to split training, inference, and burst demand, the framework in Enterprise GPU Strategy in 2026 applies directly. The geographic dimension is covered in Sovereign AI Infrastructure . Over the next decade, discovery will be written by teams that can put the right compute next to the right problem, quickly. The science is ready. Whether the infrastructure keeps pace has become a choice rather than a constraint. That market context is mapped in AI Compute Market 2026 . About Axe Compute Axe Compute Inc. Axe Compute gives enterprises and AI innovators choice across hardware, geography, and deployment speed through two delivery models: Axe Compute Access, providing the latest GPU compute options in as fast as 48 hours across numerous global locations, and Axe Compute Build, enabling enterprises to access large-scale dedicated AI factories, all backed by enterprise-grade SLAs and support. Axe Compute provides the sustained, GPU-dense capacity this work requires. What are the biggest examples of AI in science? AlphaFold predicted the structure of nearly every known protein and won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. GraphCast produces 10-day global weather forecasts that beat the leading physics-based system. GNoME predicted 2.2 million new crystals, of which about 380,000 are likely stable. Deep reinforcement learning has controlled fusion plasma in a live tokamak, and AlphaProof reached a silver-medal score at the International Mathematical Olympiad. Each runs on intensive GPU infrastructure of the kind Axe Compute provides. How is scientific AI compute different from running a large language model? This produces continuous, high-intensity GPU demand rather than spiky conversational traffic. title: Vicat’s Montalieu-Vercieu cement plant to supply CO2 for e-fuel production
summary: Vicat’s Montalieu-Vercieu cement plant to supply CO2 for e-fuel production
body_text: France: The Rhône Décarbonisation project, involving Vicat, H4 Marseille Fos, Société du Pipeline Sud-Européen (SPSE) and liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal developer Elengy, has secured 50% of the long-term biogenic CO2 supply needed for H4 Marseille Fos’ production of electrically-derived sustainable aviation fuel (e-SAF). This will come from 1.2Mt/yr of CO2 captured from Vicat’s Montalieu-Vercieu cement plant in Isère, with transport through an SPSE pipeline running for approximately 350km. The scheme, being developed by Hy2gen and H2V, will create France’s first structured carbon capture and utilisation value chain, with a final investment decision expected in 2028. H4 Marseille Fos is targeting production of 75,000t/yr of e-SAF using methanol-to-jet fuel technology from 2032 onwards. The project aims to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 240,000t/yr of CO2-eq compared to kerosene. As well as e-SAF, the project will also export e-methanol delivered by ship at Fos-sur-Mer. Ports Europe reported in February 2026 that Marseille Fos port allocated 46.6 hectares at Môle Central to H4 Marseille Fos for the €1.5bn project.

title: Essential Heat Warning for Millions Taking Blood Pressure Medicines in the UK
summary: Why people taking ACE inhibitors, beta blockers and other medicines need extra care during hot weather Millions of people across the UK who take prescription medicines have been reminded to take extra precautions during periods of hot weather. body_text: Why people taking ACE inhibitors, beta blockers and other medicines need extra care during hot weather Millions of people across the UK who take prescription medicines have been reminded to take extra precautions during periods of hot weather. Health officials have warned that high temperatures can affect both how medicines are stored and how the body responds while taking certain treatments. The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has issued advice for people using commonly prescribed medicines, including ACE inhibitors and beta blockers. These medications are widely used to manage conditions such as high blood pressure, heart problems and other long-term health conditions. As temperatures rise during summer heatwaves, patients are being encouraged to check how they store their medicines and understand whether their medication could increase their risk of heat-related problems. Which medicines are affected by hot weather? Many commonly prescribed medicines can be affected by extreme heat. ACE inhibitors and beta blockers are among the main groups highlighted by health officials. ACE inhibitors, including medicines such as ramipril, enalapril and captopril, are often prescribed to help control blood pressure and support people with heart conditions. Beta blockers, including bisoprolol, propranolol and atenolol, are also frequently prescribed for heart-related conditions, high blood pressure and other medical concerns. The MHRA has also advised people taking other types of medication to remain aware during very warm weather. These include: • Some diabetes medicines, including insulin and metformin • Diuretics, also known as water tablets, such as furosemide • Certain antidepressants and antipsychotic medicines • Some antibiotics and skin treatments that can increase sensitivity to sunlight People taking these medicines should follow medical advice and speak with a pharmacist or healthcare professional if they are concerned. How does heat affect medication? Most medicines should be stored in a cool, dry place, usually below 25C unless the packaging states otherwise. During hot weather, indoor temperatures, cars and direct sunlight can create conditions that may damage some medicines. Heat can reduce the effectiveness of certain medications by affecting their active ingredients. Medicines that need refrigeration are especially vulnerable if they are exposed to high temperatures for long periods. Leaving medication inside a parked car, near a sunny window or inside a bag exposed to sunlight could affect its quality. The MHRA advises people to check medicine labels and patient information leaflets for specific storage instructions. Why some medicines can make heat harder to manage Hot weather naturally causes the body to lose more water through sweating. However, some medicines can make it more difficult for the body to regulate temperature or recognise signs of dehydration. For example, some blood pressure medicines can affect the body's response during sudden temperature increases. ACE inhibitors may reduce thirst signals, meaning some people may not realise they need to drink more fluids. Beta blockers can also affect how the body responds to heat by influencing heart rate and circulation. Diuretics can increase fluid loss because they encourage the body to remove more water through urination. This can raise the risk of dehydration during hot conditions. People with existing health conditions, including heart disease, kidney problems or diabetes, may need to take extra care during heatwaves. Signs of dehydration and heat-related illness Recognising the early signs of dehydration is important, especially for older adults and people taking regular medication. Common symptoms can include: • Feeling dizzy or lightheaded • Headaches • Unusual tiredness • Confusion • Darker urine • Increased thirst If someone feels unwell during hot weather, they should move to a cooler area, drink fluids slowly and seek medical advice if symptoms continue or become worse. Severe heat-related illness can become dangerous quickly, particularly among vulnerable groups. Tips to protect medicines during summer The MHRA recommends several simple steps to keep medicines safe during periods of high temperatures: Store medicines correctly Keep medication in a cool, dry location away from direct sunlight. Avoid storing medicines in places that become hot, such as cars, window ledges or outdoor areas. Check storage instructions Different medicines have different requirements. Always follow the guidance on the packaging or speak to a healthcare professional if you are unsure. Avoid leaving medicines in hot vehicles A car can become extremely hot even when outdoor temperatures are moderate. Medicines left inside may be exposed to damaging levels of heat. Stay hydrated Drink enough fluids during hot weather and pay attention to signs that your body may be struggling with the temperature. Take care in the sun Some medicines can make skin more sensitive to sunlight. This may increase the chance of sunburn, so extra protection such as sunscreen, shade and suitable clothing may be needed. When should you contact a healthcare professional? People should not stop taking prescribed medication without medical advice. If you are worried about how your medicine may interact with hot weather, contact your pharmacist, GP or healthcare provider. A healthcare professional can provide guidance based on your individual circumstances and explain whether any extra precautions are needed. Final thoughts Summer heat can create additional challenges for millions of people who rely on regular medication. While most people can continue taking their prescriptions safely, it is important to understand how temperature, hydration and medicine storage can affect health. Simple steps such as storing medicines properly, drinking enough fluids and recognising warning signs can help reduce the risks during hot weather. Anyone taking ACE inhibitors, beta blockers or other long-term treatments should remain aware of official health guidance and seek advice if they have concerns. Sources Information for this article is based on guidance from the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) regarding medicine safety during periods of extreme heat, alongside general public health advice from UK healthcare organisations. Disclaimer This article is for general information purposes only and does not replace professional medical advice. Medication requirements vary from person to person. Do not stop, change or adjust prescribed medicines without speaking to a qualified healthcare professional.

title: How we built Multifactor's founding engineering team in six weeks
summary: How Multifactor designed a hiring process backward from the product it's building — treating technical depth and cultural fit as equally non-negotiable — to hire its founding engineering team in six weeks.
body_text: How we built Multifactor's founding engineering team in six weeks 2026-07-13 Company Team Hiring CS Chintan Shah Interim VP of Engineering The first thing I did when Vivek Nair asked me to help hire Multifactor's first engineers was write a rubric. That may sound counterintuitive. Most early-stage hiring starts with a req and a gut feel — you post the role, you read résumés, and tell yourself you'll know the right person when you see them. But when you're a founder, "I'll know it when I see it" is not a direction you can hand off to someone else — it lives in one person's head, and a bar that lives in one person's head gets applied slowly, inconsistently, and only by the founder. Some context. Multifactor (YC F25) is rebuilding the identity layer of the internet for the AI era — cryptographic infrastructure that lets people and their AI agents share access to online accounts without ever exposing credentials. Turn any account into a shareable, revocable, cryptographically guaranteed permission link. The company had just closed a $15M seed led by Nexus Venture Partners, with Y Combinator, Taurus Ventures, and Pioneer Fund in the round. Abhishek Sharma at Nexus, who led the deal, introduced me to Vivek. The science is unusually real — peer-reviewed at USENIX Security, presented at DEF CON, a decade of patents underneath it — which set an unusually high bar for who could build on top of it. We needed engineers with genuine security depth and genuine AI-agent depth, at startup speed. That combination is rare, and a lazy résumé filter would have thrown away most of the people who actually had it. Two beliefs shaped everything that followed: that a recruiting process should be designed backward from what the company is building, and that for a founding team, technical depth and cultural fit matter in equal measure. Hiring your first engineers is an inexact science. Survey ten founders who've been through it and you'll get ten different answers on their approach — and timing and context matter too, since what worked a year ago might not work today. What follows are the principles that worked for us, in case they're useful to other early-stage teams doing the same thing. First, I used the product Before I wrote a word of the rubric, I did the thing I'd tell any technical advisor to do first: I used the product. Vivek's team had built a working proof-of-concept during YC, and I spent real time using it — not just listening to the pitch. That turned out to be the most useful step in the whole process. Understanding the product at that level is what made every downstream decision easier to get right. It told me what the team actually needed to be — which pillars mattered, and how much — so the rubric described this product's problem instead of a generic senior engineer. It shaped the interview itself — the live coding briefs were slices of our real surface rather than abstract puzzles. It told me who to look for and where to find them. And it meant I could explain Multifactor to candidates myself — the vision, why it matters, why now — and get them genuinely excited without routing every conversation through the founder. On an early team, the founder's time is the scarcest resource there is; having someone else carry the product context made the whole process faster and let Vivek spend his hours where only he could. You can't hire well for a product you don't understand. So I made understanding it step zero — and then I wrote the bar down. Step one: decide what "great" actually means The easy part was writing the Founding Engineer and Engineering Lead role definitions. The hard part: turning "great for Multifactor" into an explicit, six-pillar rubric. Security, cryptography, and identity systems. AI, ML, and agent systems. Systems level thinking. Practical engineering choices. Academic and research signal. Startup, zero-to-one execution. Hiring is not a one-size-fits-all process. These pillars were designed around Multifactor's product and the challenges we foresaw getting it to market: you cannot build a zero-trust identity product for AI agents without someone who has actually built security systems, and you cannot build for the agentic web without someone who has actually built with LLMs and agents. Each pillar had explicit tiers — what a 7 looked like versus a 17 versus a 22 — with named companies, named teams, and named signals. The point wasn't false precision. It was to force the fuzzy judgment out of my head and onto paper, where it could be applied the same way to the hundredth candidate as to the first. And the first version wasn't the one we used. A hiring bar is a product, and like any product it took iterations: we tuned pillar weights, rewrote tiers that were too vague to apply consistently, and recalibrated against real candidates as they came in. It didn't fully settle until the end of the second week. The founders who expect to write a perfect scorecard on day one are usually the ones who abandon it by day three — the point is to start rough and sharpen it against reality. This is, quietly, the same discipline the product itself demands. In security, an idea that lives only in the architect's intuition is an idea that gets implemented inconsistently. So is a hiring bar. Step two: prime the pipeline — and give it three weeks Sourcing was deliberately wide. YC's Work at a Startup gave us volume. Warm referrals — from investors, from university networks, from the team — gave us signal, and we tracked every candidate back to the exact person who referred them, because provenance matters a lot when you're calibrating trust. LinkedIn and direct inbound filled in the rest. Founders can sometimes give up on the funnel too soon. They want it humming on day one, but sourcing is a spring you load before it releases — for the first couple of weeks it looks like nothing is happening, just quiet on the other end. By the end of week two we saw the first real movement: candidates writing back, reserving slots for intro calls. It took a full three weeks before the pipeline was genuinely humming. That lag is normal, and the founders who panic through it — lowering the bar to manufacture the feeling of progress — are trading away their single most important early decision. Step three: review the flood without drowning A written bar has a second payoff: you can partially automate against it. As résumés came in, we structured them and scored each candidate against the rubric — and we did it with two independent frontier models rather than one. Where both models agreed, we had a fast, high-confidence read. Where they disagreed, the disagreement itself was the signal to put a human on it. That's the same fail-closed instinct we hold in the product: automate the easy, confident cases; route the ambiguous ones to a person; never let the machine make a silent, irreversible call it isn't sure about. It let a small, part-time recruiting effort keep pace with a large inbound without ever letting a strong candidate fall through on autopilot — and it decided who was worth a live conversation in the first place. Step four: how to interview engineers when everyone codes with AI Coding interviews have taken on a different meaning in the age of AI coding tools. Every serious candidate now has Cursor, Claude, and Copilot. Which means the classic screen — can you produce a correct algorithm on demand — now tests the one thing the machine already does well. If a model can ace your interview, you are no longer measuring the candidate. You're measuring their tools. Making the question harder doesn't fix it — it just moves the problem: ratchet up the difficulty and the model clears that bar too, and all you've done is raise everyone's score by the same amount. So we did the opposite of what the automated tools do. No take-home, no timed leetcode, no proctored puzzle — a live, 60-minute paired-programming session with me. Candidates got a short prep guide beforehand so they knew exactly what to expect, and the brief itself at the top of the call. The problems were slices of our real product surface — build an end-to-end-encrypted file-sharing flow where the server can never read the contents; build an internal tool that surfaces potential PII across messy, multi-source data — spanning backend and frontend, in whatever stack they liked. AI tools weren't just allowed; they were encouraged. But before writing a line, each candidate walked me through their plan — which tool for which part, and how they'd stay in control of what it generated — and then we built together while I asked about every meaningful piece of code. That's the whole test: not whether the AI can write it, but whether the human can own it — steer it, catch its mistakes, defend the trade-offs, and cut the right scope when the clock is short. Two things mattered more than I expected. First, the human on the other end. Candidates are increasingly alienated by this new breed of LLM-powered interview bots — one-way recordings, automated scorers, nobody actually watching. A real person pairing with them is both more respectful and more revealing: you see how they think out loud, how they collaborate, how they react when something breaks. Second, we let AI do the part humans are bad at — every session was captured by an AI notetaker (Fathom) so I could give the candidate my full attention instead of scribbling notes. AI assisting the evaluation; a human making the call. The same pattern we used everywhere. I was much more interested in the choices they made than the actual code that was ultimately written. Did they reach for a vetted crypto library or try to roll their own? Where did they put the trust boundary? When they had to cut scope — and everyone cuts scope in sixty minutes — did they cut the right things, and say so out loud? Could they explain a tradeoff to a non-expert and defend a protocol choice to one? Those are the signals that predict whether someone can turn a research paper into correct-by-construction production code. None of them come out of a prompt. Step five: fly the finalists to San Francisco The remote session proved someone could build. The on-site was for everything you can only judge in person — so we flew the finalists to the San Francisco office for a day built around three things. The first was systems thinking : an open-ended whiteboard design problem — an AI system in a regulated, customer-facing domain — worked through out loud, together. We weren't after the "right" architecture, but how they scoped it before drawing, how they reasoned about trade-offs and failure modes, and whether they went deep where it mattered instead of surveying everything. The second was the perspective of the person on the other end . In a regulated, customer-facing domain, the tell was whether they raised privacy, compliance, explainability, and human review unprompted — designing for the user, not just the diagram. A live coding module, scoped from their own design, then showed us they could build a real slice of what they'd just proposed. The third was judgment about their own experience . Senior engineers carry strong priors; the best ones know when not to apply them. We looked for people who drew on hard-won experience but picked the right tool for this problem — who didn't reach for an LLM by default just because their last company did. The rubric had six pillars on paper. Cultural fit was the seventh — the one you can't score in a spreadsheet, and we weighted it just as heavily. A founding hire has to fit the people, not only the problem, so candidates spent real time with more than Vivek — the founding designer and Leslie, our chief of staff. I'd worked with Leslie on a set of culture questions, and instead of marching through a checklist she wove them into real conversation. Candidates left with a genuine feel for what working at Multifactor is like — the people, not just the technical challenge. Culture fit, judged in both directions: an offer went out only when someone cleared the bar and the team wanted to build alongside them. Treat every candidate like you'll meet them again One thing we treated as non-negotiable: every candidate should leave the process better than they came in — offer or not. Not out of politeness. The engineers you most want are already being courted by other companies and weighing several options at once; for them, the interview is part of your pitch. How your process feels is the clearest preview a candidate gets of what working with you will actually be like. So we made it personal and kept it a real conversation, not a gauntlet — and the whole team leaned in, not just the interviewers of record. Candidates met the actual people they'd build with and got an honest read on the place instead of a recruiter's script. That effort is what made the process feel alive rather than transactional, and the strongest candidates noticed. When someone has four other offers, that feeling is often the deciding factor. The payoff also outlasts any single decision. People remember how they were treated long after they've forgotten the coding brief. Candidates we passed on have sent us referrals; some are people we'd want to work with down the road; all of them describe the experience to other engineers. In a small world where the best people all know each other, a great process compounds — treating candidates well is the highest-return recruiting investment there is. The result: a founding team in six weeks Once the spring released, it released fast. Referrals compounded, the paired sessions and the on-site rounds did the filtering résumés couldn't, and the offers went out. We went from no engineers to a founding team in six weeks — and, more importantly, to a team , not a set of individually impressive résumés. The pillars were a deliberate hedge against monoculture: security-native, AI-native, and startup-speed, balanced across people who make each other better. The bar had one more effect I didn't expect. It was so specific — deep security and deep AI-agent experience — that some of the strongest people who cleared it weren't looking for a job at all. They were founders already building a piece of this problem. That's how we met Dave Blumenfeld . He'd started Keypo, attacking the secure-enclave side of exactly what we do — using trusted execution environments so an agent can use a credential without ever seeing it, the natural complement to Multifactor's key-derivation work. Dave was a fit in three ways at once: he cleared the engineering bar, he'd been building the other half of our technology, and he had the zero-to-one instinct of someone who'd done it before. The moment the overlap was obvious, a hire turned into something bigger, and Keypo joined Multifactor . The search didn't just find us engineers; it surfaced a fit deep enough to combine two companies. That team is now heads-down shipping V1, and I'm in it with them as interim VP of Engineering. One seat left The founding engineering team is complete. The one remaining founding seat is the hardest one: a Founding Chief Scientist — a founding executive who will own Multifactor's genuinely unsolved problems and carry the answers all the way into production. Fine-grained delegated authorization for AI agents. Cryptographic delegation at scale. Provable, natural-language auditing of what an agent actually did with your account. None of these has a known answer yet. If that's the kind of problem you've spent your life running toward, we should talk. The smarter agents get, the more of your life they'll touch — and the more it matters who's building the layer that stands between them and everything you own. That's the bar this team was hired against. — Chintan We're redefining zero-trust — so you can protect your accounts with confidence. Identity is your first and last line of defense, and the root cause of most application security breaches. Multifactor's provably secure zero-trust solutions cryptographically guarantee that only authorized users can access sensitive data, turning identity into your greatest asset in the fight against cyber threats. title: Salesforce Pricing 2026: Plans, Costs, and What You'll Actually Pay
summary: Explore Salesforce pricing in 2026: plans, costs, and everything you need to know.
body_text: TL;DR: Salesforce's prices vary by product line and additional costs. Plan carefully to avoid surprises. Salesforce Pricing 2026: Plans, Costs, and What You'll Actually Pay Last updated: August 2026 The top salesforce pricing are Sales Cloud (enhancing sales processes), Service Cloud (customer support management), Marketing Cloud (marketing campaign personalization). Salesforce continues to be a dominant CRM platform, but understanding its pricing structure is crucial for any business considering it. Recent updates have introduced more variability in costs, prompting businesses to look closely at what they'll actually pay. What are Salesforce's current pricing plans? Salesforce pricing is extensive and tailored to a variety of business needs, from small enterprise solutions to comprehensive CRM management tools. Each product line, including Sales Cloud and Marketing Cloud, comes with its unique pricing tiers. These tiers reflect the level of features and scalability, but understanding the complete cost structure is essential to fully appreciate what Salesforce offers. Salesforce pricing table: A detailed breakdown The Salesforce pricing for 2026 features diverse plans tailored to varying business needs across its product suite. For the Sales Cloud, monthly prices range from $25 for the Essentials plan to $300 for the Unlimited plan, each offering progressively more features suitable for sales teams' different sizes and requirements. Similarly, the Service Cloud offers its Starter at $25 per user per month and scales up to $300 for the Unlimited plan, making it suitable for businesses with varying CRM demands. Marketing Cloud prices are custom. You’ll need to contact Salesforce for a quote that fits your specific marketing needs. Sales Cloud Salesforce's Sales Cloud is ideal for enhancing sales processes. It offers a range of pricing plans designed to cater to businesses of different scales. The foundational Essentials plan costs $25 per user per month, which includes basic sales engagement tools. The Professional plan at $75 per user monthly introduces team collaboration tools, ideal for growing teams. At $150 per month per user, the Enterprise option offers deeper insights for strategic decision-making with advanced analytics. For full customization and support, the Unlimited plan at $300 monthly per user opens doors to exclusive support and configures sales processes extensively. Best for: All-encompassing sales management Key features: Contact and opportunity management Sales forecasting and analytics Email integration with Outlook and Gmail Advanced reporting and dashboards The Sales Cloud shines in its ability to scale with your business, offering tools for smooth integration with email platforms and in-depth analytics. However, the cost may escalate with additional requirements. Service Cloud The Service Cloud is tailored for customer support excellence. Starting at $25 per user monthly with the Essentials plan, it provides a base for handling customer inquiries efficiently. Its Professional and Enterprise plans, priced at $75 and $150 per user per month respectively, introduce features like case management and workflows for larger support teams. With the Unlimited tier at $300 per month per user, businesses can use complete 24/7 support along with augmented AI tools. Best for: Robust customer service operations Key features: Case management and workflow automation Multi-channel support (email, social media) Knowledge base management Integration with AI for customer interaction insights The Service Cloud ensures comprehensive customer service but may come with a steep learning curve due to its extensive features. Marketing Cloud The Marketing Cloud is structured to cater to personalized and data-driven marketing campaigns. Pricing for this tool is highly variable and requires direct consultation with Salesforce, supporting enterprises with grand marketing ambitions. Best for: Personalized marketing campaigns Key features: Campaign management tools Audience segmentation Integration with third-party platforms AI-driven content personalization While it offers superior capabilities in customizing campaigns, the complexity and potential total cost might constrain smaller teams. Salesforce's pricing tiers are structured to accommodate varying degrees of complexity and team sizes. For businesses navigating Salesforce's extensive options, exploring their specific needs alongside these plans is advisable to avoid unnecessary expenditures. How Salesforce's billing model works Salesforce's billing model is fundamentally based on per-user licensing and varies significantly depending on the features and usage tiers selected. This structured approach often means that the more robust the functionality a business requires, the higher the cost tends to be. The pricing can quickly escalate as companies scale their operations and require more licenses or additional features. The per-user licensing model used by Salesforce can lead to significant expenses, especially for larger teams. Each user typically requires a separate license, resulting in multiplying costs as the team expands. This stands in contrast to CRM solutions like Miniloop, which offer flat fees and eliminate per-seat charges. Salesforce's model can be advantageous for businesses that need specific advanced features for a smaller number of users, but becomes a financial strain as the team size increases. Moreover, with Salesforce, businesses often face the dilemma of feature overload or underuse. Picture a company that only needs basic CRM functionalities but opts for a higher-tier package anticipating growth. They might end up paying for advanced features they rarely use. Alternatively, selecting a lower-tier package might limit their capabilities, potentially requiring costly upgrades later on. This careful balancing act of feature selection against cost and utility is a frequent challenge for businesses using Salesforce. In addition to selecting the right tier, it's essential to consider the broader implications of Salesforce's structured pricing. Utilizing a comprehensive CRM like Salesforce means factoring in potential additional costs, such as implementation, third-party integrations, and ongoing support, which can accumulate and impact your budget significantly. Often, businesses underestimate these associated expenses, resulting in budget overshoots. When considering Salesforce, it's crucial for businesses to have a clear understanding of their current needs and projected growth. While its feature-rich environment can be highly beneficial, the pricing model requires careful analysis to avoid unnecessary costs. For those seeking more tailored solutions, exploring alternatives might be worthwhile. HubSpot vs Salesforce (2026): Pricing, Features, Which CRM Is Better could provide additional insights into how different CRMs stack up against Salesforce.
